q-130025:
First, notice that the domain $R$ can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =S\cup T\cup U.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{S}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}0\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

q-130038:
First, notice that the rectangle $R$ can be represented as a union of two smaller rectangles, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =(1,2)\times ((1,2)\cup (2,4)) \\  & =((1,2)\times (1,2))\cup ((1,2)\times (2,4)).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{(1,2)\times (1,2)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(1,2)\times (2,4)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{(1,2)\times (1,2)}\frac{y+1}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(1,2)\times (2,4)}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

q-81253:
First, notice that we have $R={R}_{1}\cup {R}_{2}$, where ${R}_{1}=(-1,1)\times (0,\pi )$ and ${R}_{2}=(1,2)\times (0,\pi ).$ So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A= & ={∬}_{{R}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{R}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{{R}_{1}}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{R}_{2}}x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}A \\  & =(1-(-1)){\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y+({\int }_{1}^{2}x\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y) \\  & =2[\operatorname{sin}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi }+[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]_{1}^{2}\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =2(0)+(2-\frac{1}{2})\cdot (-(-1)+1) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

q-40727:
First, let's represent $D$ as a type I region. To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14100085/assets/da2895c09bc33f628626257b6d102e74875825df14ba744904e02ffa71552a02.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,2{x}^{2}\le y\le 1+{x}^{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{2{x}^{2}}^{1+{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[{\int }_{2{x}^{2}}^{1+{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\,dy]dx\end{aligned}
$$

q-132117:
First, let's represent $D$ as a type I region. To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14100085/assets/8df9c4544478d7146dbcb1790c8ed9a9f57cd1e52b1f50a8b344c2aa0551fa90.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,{x}^{3}\le y\le \sqrt[3]{x}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{3}}^{\sqrt[3]{x}}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{{x}^{3}}^{\sqrt[3]{x}}f(x,y)\,dy]dx\end{aligned}
$$

q-132249:
First, let's make a sketch of our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14100085/assets/24d3b93e82e88bb581eff3005687ae4ee3dc3ae0d6c25fbc26f72665042ae5c6.png)

Now, let's represent $D$ as a type I region. 

- To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-x+6 & =2x \\ 3x & =6 \\ x & =\frac{6}{3} \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x$-limits are 
$0\le x\le 2.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14100085/assets/af61865f54494840090351296e8a1c21446787ca0b273005e7bf9c2907585adb.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,2x\le y\le 6-x\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{2x}^{6-x}f(x,y)\text{ }dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$
